# Data Frames

```{r df}
crashes_by_day = c(2020, 2241, 2327, 2285, 2380, 1866, 1664)
names(crashes_by_day) = c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu",
                          "Fri", "Sat", "Sun")

crashes_df = tibble::tibble(
  day = names(crashes_by_day),
  crashes = crashes_by_day,
  busy = crashes_by_day > 2000
)
crashes_df

dplyr::glimpse(crashes_df) #equivalent of str() but prints neater
```

# Examining the Job Ad

```{r job_ad}
job = list(
  title   = "Research Data Scientist, Magic Eye",
  company = "Google",
  salary  = list(min = 147000, max = 210000)
)
str(job)

# Write one expression to extract each of the company name, the maximum salary, the maximum salary again using only [[]], and the names of the elements in job

# 1. The company name
company_name = job$company # job[[2]]; however, this returns a list job [2]
company_name_as_named_list = job[2] # we typically don't want that as an answer

# 2. The maximum salary
max_salary = job$salary$max

# 3. Max salary using only square brackets
job[[3]][[2]] # use 3 because salary is the third criteria, 2 is going to return the second subelement from that list

# 4. Names of the elements in job.
names(job)

```

## Vectors
- You can subset by position (i.e., a number) or by name if it is a named vector;
- You can also pass a vector (e.g., logical condition 2:4 or c()) for subsetting the vector
```{r vectors}
crashes_by_day = c(2020, 2241, 2327, 2285, 2380, 1866, 1664)
names(crashes_by_day) = c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu",
                          "Fri", "Sat", "Sun")
crashes_by_day[2:4] # you can give consecutive numbers
crashes_by_day[c('Mon', 'Fri')] # crashes_by_day[c(1,5)]
```
